Estimates a model of the evolution of prevalences of disability by age

Source: R/fitPrevalenceModel.R
fitPrevalenceModel.Rd

Estimates, on past observations of prevalences of disability by age, a model that can then be used to project prevalences (see predict.prevalence_model). Four methods are available.

Usage

fitPrevalenceModel(
  tab,
  method = c("trend", "mortality", "target", "shift"),
  fit_years = NULL,
  exclude_years = NULL,
  categories = NULL,
  scale = c("logit", "log", "level"),
  estimator = c("ols", "endpoints"),
  slope = c("common", "by_age"),
  age_lag = 0,
  eps = 1e-06,
  indicator = c("dle", "dfle", "pct_dle", "pct_dfle", "ratio"),
  rule = c("constant", "trend", "horizon"),
  scope = c("all_ages", "min_age"),
  ref_year = NULL,
  change = NULL,
  horizon = NULL,
  after = c("linear", "constant"),
  anchor_age = NULL,
  uniform_scale = c("odds", "level"),
  from_age = NULL,
  n_extrap = 5
)

Arguments

tab

a data frame with variables 'year', 'age' (single years of age) and 'pix' (prevalence), plus 'qx' (mortality rate) if method is "mortality" or "target". Optional variables 'sex' and 'categ', and the variables listed in 'categories', define separate series: one model is estimated for each series, and each series must contain the same ages for all years. Prevalences can be obtained for example with ApproxPrevalenceTable.

method

"trend", "mortality", "target" or "shift" (see Details)

fit_years

vector of the years used for the estimation (default: all years of 'tab')

exclude_years

vector of years to be left out of the estimation (for example the years of a crisis)

categories

names of variables of 'tab' defining separate series (in addition to 'sex' and 'categ' when they exist)

scale

scale on which prevalences are modelled: "logit" (default, keeps projected prevalences between 0 and 1), "log" or "level" (prevalences themselves)

estimator

method "trend", or method "target" with rule "trend": "ols" (default) or "endpoints" (slope between the first and the last years)

slope

method "mortality" only: "common" (default) for a single slope \(\beta\), or "by_age"

age_lag

method "mortality" only: age shift \(k\) (in years of age) between the age of prevalences and the age of the mortality rates (default 0). A vector selects the best value (see Details).

eps

with scale "logit" or "log", prevalences below 'eps' (or, with "logit", above 1 - 'eps') are replaced by this bound, with a warning

indicator

method "target" only: "dle", "dfle", "pct_dle", "pct_dfle" or "ratio" (see Details)

rule

method "target" only: "constant", "trend" or "horizon" (see Details)

scope

method "target" only: "all_ages" (a target at each age) or "min_age" (uniform evolution of prevalences, see Details)

ref_year

methods "target" (rules "constant" and "horizon") and "shift": reference year (default: last year of the estimation)

change

method "target", rule "horizon": relative change of the indicator, in percent, between the reference year and 'horizon'

horizon

method "target", rule "horizon": year at which the change is reached

after

method "target", rule "horizon": "linear" (default, the change goes on at the same pace after 'horizon') or "constant"

anchor_age

method "target", scope "min_age": age at which the hypothesis is applied (default: minimum age)

uniform_scale

method "target", scope "min_age": "odds" (default) or "level" (see Details)

from_age

method "target", scope "all_ages": age from which the hypothesis is applied (default NULL: all ages, see Details)

n_extrap

method "shift": number of ages used to extrapolate the curve beyond the first and the last ages (default 5)

Value

an object of class "prevalence_model", a list containing in particular the data frames 'coefficients' (one row per series, age and term; see coef.prevalence_model), 'fitted', 'fit_stats' and 'observed'. Use predict.prevalence_model to project prevalences, and the other methods listed in coef.prevalence_model to retrieve the results of the estimation.

Details

Method "trend" extrapolates prevalences at each age (separately). Denoting \(p_{a,t}\) the prevalence at age \(a\) and year \(t\) and \(g\) the transformation defined by 'scale' (logit, log or identity): $$g(p_{a,t}) = \alpha_a + \beta_a (t - t_0) + \varepsilon_{a,t}$$ where \(t_0\) is the last year used for the estimation. With estimator = "ols", coefficients are estimated by ordinary least squares over all the years used for the estimation; with estimator = "endpoints", the slope is calculated from the first and the last years only.

Method "mortality" links the evolution of prevalences to the evolution of mortality rates \(q_{a,t}\). If disability occurs on average \(k\) years before death, a decrease of mortality at age \(a+k\) should translate into a decrease of the prevalence of disability at age \(a\): $$g(p_{a,t}) = \alpha_a + \beta \ln q_{a+k,t} + \varepsilon_{a,t}$$ The intercepts \(\alpha_a\) are specific to each age. The slope \(\beta\) is common to all ages if slope = "common" (the default), or specific to each age (\(\beta_a\)) if slope = "by_age" (more flexible, but noisier). The age shift \(k\) is given by 'age_lag' (in years of age, not necessarily an integer: \(\ln q\) is interpolated linearly between ages). If 'age_lag' is a vector, the value that minimises the sum of squared residuals is retained (separately for each series, see 'categories'). This is a descriptive criterion, not a statistical test. For ages \(a\) such that \(a+k\) is higher than the last age of the table, the mortality rate of the last age is used.

Method "shift" assumes that the curve of prevalences by age of a reference year \(t_0\) moves towards older ages at a constant speed \(s\) (in years of age per calendar year): $$\mathrm{logit}\,p_{a,t} = \mathrm{logit}\,p_{a - s\,(t - t_0),\,t_0}$$ For each year \(t\) of the estimation, the shift \(d_t\) that brings the curve of the reference year closest to the curve of year \(t\) is searched (least squares on the logit of prevalences); \(s\) is the slope of the regression of \(d_t\) on \(t - t_0\), without intercept (since \(d_{t_0} = 0\)). The \(d_t\) are available with as.data.frame(model, what = "shifts"). Values between ages are interpolated linearly (on the logit scale), and the curve is extrapolated linearly beyond the first and the last ages, using the slope estimated on the 'n_extrap' first (or last) ages. This is a simple hypothesis: a single speed is assumed for all ages, whereas observed shifts are usually faster at some ages than at others, so that the method can be a poor representation of observed evolutions.

Method "target" projects prevalences from a hypothesis on life expectancies, with the Sullivan method (see also prevalenceForecast). Denote EVI the life expectancy with disability at age \(a\) and year \(t\), EVSI the disability-free life expectancy and \(e = EVI + EVSI\) the total life expectancy. The hypothesis is made of three choices:

  • the indicator : "dle" (EVI), "dfle" (EVSI), "pct_dle" (share of EVI in total life expectancy, in percent, \(100\,EVI/e\)), "pct_dfle" (share of EVSI) or "ratio" (EVSI/EVI). A linear evolution of "pct_dle" and of "pct_dfle" are equivalent hypotheses; this is not the case for a relative change (rule "horizon"), nor for "dle" and "dfle" (since \(e\) does not evolve linearly).

  • the rule giving the value of the indicator \(v_{a,t}\) in the projection years: "constant" (\(v_{a,t} = v_{a,t_0}\), with \(t_0\) the reference year 'ref_year'); "trend" (linear extrapolation of the indicator at each age, estimated over the years of the estimation, with 'estimator'); "horizon" (the indicator changes by 'change' percent between the reference year and the year 'horizon', linearly in between: \(v_{a,t} = v_{a,t_0}\,[1 + (change/100)\,(t - t_0)/(horizon - t_0)]\); after 'horizon' the change goes on linearly (after = "linear") or stops (after = "constant")).

  • the scope: with scope = "all_ages", the rule is applied at each age, which gives a targeted EVI at each age; prevalences are the ones that give this EVI, given the projected mortality (inversion of the Sullivan method, as in prevalenceForecast). At the youngest ages, where prevalences are very low, the inversion is unstable and can require negative prevalences. If 'from_age' is given, the hypothesis is only applied to the ages \(a \ge\) 'from_age', and prevalences of younger ages follow the evolution of the odds at age 'from_age': \(\mathrm{logit}\,p_{a,t} = \mathrm{logit}\,p_{a,t_0} + [\mathrm{logit}\,p_{a_0,t} - \mathrm{logit}\,p_{a_0,t_0}]\) (the hypothesis is then not satisfied at ages below 'from_age'). With scope = "min_age", the rule is only applied at the minimum age (or at 'anchor_age'), and prevalences of all ages evolve uniformly, from those of the reference year, so that the targeted EVI at this age is reached: the odds of prevalences are multiplied by the same factor at all ages (uniform_scale = "odds", prevalences always remain between 0 and 1) or prevalences are multiplied by the same factor, with a maximum of 1 (uniform_scale = "level"). This is a theoretical hypothesis, as prevalences do not usually evolve in the same proportion at all ages.

With method "target", 'tab' must also contain mortality rates for all the ages of the life table, up to its last age (consecutive years of age), and the estimation does not transform prevalences ('scale' is not used). Prevalences "fitted" by the model are the ones implied by the hypothesis with the observed mortality of each year (for rule "constant", they are the observed prevalences at the reference year); residuals are differences of logits. A hypothesis may be impossible to satisfy with the projected mortality: see argument 'on_unfeasible' of predict.prevalence_model.

See also

predict.prevalence_model, projectPrevalence, prevalenceForecast

Examples

# prevalences by age (simulated) : the odds of disability decrease by 2 percent a year at age 80, 1 percent at age 60
ages <- 60:100; years <- 2010:2019
obs <- expand.grid(age = ages, year = years)
obs$pix <- plogis(-6 + 0.12 * (obs$age - 60) - (0.01 + 0.0005 * (obs$age - 60)) * (obs$year - 2019))

m <- fitPrevalenceModel(obs, method = "trend", fit_years = 2010:2019)
m
#> Model of prevalences by age, method "trend" (scale: logit)
#>   Years used for the estimation: 2010 to 2019 (10 years)
#>   Series: 1
#>   Ages: 60 to 100
#>   Estimator: ols
#> Use coef(), as.data.frame(, what = ) and predict() to retrieve results and project prevalences.
head(coef(m))                       # coefficients by age
#>   age      term estimate    std.error  n
#> 1  60 intercept    -6.00 2.610151e-16 10
#> 2  61 intercept    -5.88 0.000000e+00 10
#> 3  62 intercept    -5.76 0.000000e+00 10
#> 4  63 intercept    -5.64 0.000000e+00 10
#> 5  64 intercept    -5.52 0.000000e+00 10
#> 6  65 intercept    -5.40 5.536967e-16 10

# prevalences of the APA by single year of age, 2010-2024 (smoothing of the 6 age brackets, weighted by the population)
apa <- FRAPAprevalence[FRAPAprevalence$decomp == 6, c("year", "age", "prevalence")]
pop <- aggregate(popx ~ year + age0101, FRInseePopulation[FRInseePopulation$geo == "france" & FRInseePopulation$age0101 %in% 60:99, ], sum)
names(pop) <- c("year", "age", "popx")
pix <- ApproxPrevalenceTable(apa, agecuts = seq(60, 85, 5), agemin = 60, agemax = 99, weights.tab = pop, categories = "year")
#> 'prevalence' is used as prevalence variable.
pix <- data.frame(year = pix$year, age = pix$age, pix = pix$prevalence.approx)
# extension up to age 104 (prevalence constant after age 99)
pix <- rbind(pix, do.call(rbind, lapply(100:104, function(a) transform(pix[pix$age == 99, ], age = a))))

# link with mortality: the age shift between disability and death is searched between 0 and 6 years
mort <- FRInseeMortalityrates
mort <- mort[mort$sex == "all" & mort$geo == "france" & !is.na(mort$age) & mort$age %in% 60:104 &
             mort$year %in% 2010:2019, c("year", "age", "qx")]
mort$qx[mort$age == 104] <- 1
m2 <- fitPrevalenceModel(merge(pix, mort, by = c("year", "age")), method = "mortality",
                         fit_years = 2010:2019, age_lag = seq(0, 6, by = 0.5))
summary(m2)
#> Model of prevalences by age, method "mortality" (scale: logit)
#> Years used for the estimation: 2010 to 2019  
#> Age shift k: 0.5 
#> 
#> Slope on ln(q):
#>  estimate std.error
#>       1.6   0.07121
#> 
#> Fit statistics by series (sigma: residual standard deviation on the scale of the estimation):
#>  n_obs n_ages n_years   sigma     r2
#>    450     45      10 0.04026 0.5554
as.data.frame(m2, what = "lag_search")
#>    age_lag       rss selected
#> 1      0.0 0.6803797    FALSE
#> 2      0.5 0.6547633     TRUE
#> 3      1.0 0.6932980    FALSE
#> 4      1.5 0.6744808    FALSE
#> 5      2.0 0.7179977    FALSE
#> 6      2.5 0.7018281    FALSE
#> 7      3.0 0.7443353    FALSE
#> 8      3.5 0.7310730    FALSE
#> 9      4.0 0.7738706    FALSE
#> 10     4.5 0.7641225    FALSE
#> 11     5.0 0.8076077    FALSE
#> 12     5.5 0.8025072    FALSE
#> 13     6.0 0.8471726    FALSE

# horizontal shift of the curve of prevalences by age
m3 <- fitPrevalenceModel(pix, method = "shift", fit_years = 2010:2019)
coef(m3)                                  # years of age per calendar year
#>   age  term   estimate   std.error n
#> 1  NA shift 0.07008925 0.004306869 9
as.data.frame(m3, what = "shifts")
#>    year   shift_obs   shift_fit
#> 1  2010 -0.64939426 -0.63080329
#> 2  2011 -0.61264976 -0.56071404
#> 3  2012 -0.51574784 -0.49062478
#> 4  2013 -0.45553188 -0.42053553
#> 5  2014 -0.30314299 -0.35044627
#> 6  2015 -0.26962993 -0.28035702
#> 7  2016 -0.04293830 -0.21026776
#> 8  2017 -0.06282677 -0.14017851
#> 9  2018 -0.03756193 -0.07008925
#> 10 2019  0.00000000  0.00000000
